Even where Congress does not expressly preempt state action, such action may be impliedly pre-empted. 
States cannot constitutionally pass laws that interfere with the accomplishment of the purposes of the 
federal law. Suppose, for example, that Congress passes a comprehensive law that sets standards for 
foreign vessels to enter the navigable waters and ports of the United States. If a state creates a law that 
sets standards that conflict with the federal law or sets standards so burdensome that they interfere with 
federal law, the doctrine of preemption will (in accordance with the supremacy clause) void the state 
law or whatever parts of it are inconsistent with federal law. 
 
But Congress can allow what might appear to be inconsistencies; the existence of federal statutory 
standards does not always mean that local and state standards cannot be more stringent. If California 
wants cleaner air or water than other states, it can set stricter standards—nothing in the Clean Water Act 
or Clean Air Act forbids the state from setting stricter pollution standards. As the auto industry well 
knows, California has set stricter standards for auto emissions. Since the 1980s, most automakers have 
made both a federal car and a California car, because federal Clean Air Act emissions restrictions do not 
preempt more rigorous state standards. 
 
Large industries and companies actually prefer regulation at the national level. It is easier for a large 
company or industry association to lobby in Washington, DC, than to lobby in fifty different states. 
Accordingly, industry often asks Congress to put preemptive language into its statutes. The tobacco 
industry is a case in point.

qa_pairs.question: How does the doctrine of preemption affect state laws that conflict with federal laws, and can states set stricter standards than federal laws in certain areas?
qa_pairs.answer: The doctrine of preemption affects state laws by voiding any state law that conflicts with federal laws or interferes with the accomplishment of federal purposes, as per the supremacy clause. However, states can set stricter standards than federal laws in certain areas, provided that federal statutes do not explicitly forbid it. For instance, the Clean Water Act and Clean Air Act do not prevent states from establishing more stringent pollution standards. California's ability to set stricter auto emissions standards under the Clean Air Act exemplifies this principle. The federal government often includes preemptive language in statutes to prevent states from enacting laws that could undermine federal objectives. Nonetheless, industries and companies may prefer national regulation due to the ease of lobbying at the federal level, as seen in the case of the tobacco industry.

However, the FAA's preemption doctrine suggests that state laws that interfere with the federal policy of promoting arbitration are likely to be preempted. In Cippolone v. Liggett Group, the Supreme Court held that state laws that impose additional requirements on arbitration agreements are preempted by the FAA. Therefore, while the Alabama law's intent to protect consumers is commendable, it may be preempted by the FAA because it imposes additional requirements that could be seen as interfering with the federal policy favoring arbitration. The court would need to balance the state's interest in protecting consumers with the federal interest in maintaining a uniform policy that promotes arbitration as an efficient and effective alternative to litigation.

We have already seen the Fourteenth Amendment’s application in Burger King v. Rudzewicz (Section 3.9 
"Cases"). In that case, the court considered whether it was constitutionally correct for a court to assert 
personal jurisdiction over a nonresident. The states cannot constitutionally award a judgment against a 
nonresident if doing so would offend traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice. Even if the 
state’s long-arm statute would seem to allow such a judgment, other states should not give it full faith and 
credit (see Article V of the Constitution). In short, a state’s long-arm statute cannot confer personal 
jurisdiction that the state cannot constitutionally claim. 
 
The Bill of Rights (the first ten amendments to the Constitution) was originally meant to apply to federal 
actions only. During the twentieth century, the court began to apply selected rights to state action as well. 
So, for example, federal agents were prohibited from using evidence seized in violation of the Fourth 
Amendment, but state agents were not, until Mapp v. Ohio (1960), when the court applied the guarantees 
(rights) of the Fourth Amendment to state action as well. In this and in similar cases, the Fourteenth 
Amendment’s due process clause was the basis for the court’s action. The due process clause commanded 
that states provide due process in cases affecting the life, liberty, or property of US citizens, and the court 
saw in this command certain “fundamental guarantees” that states would have to observe. Over the years, 
most of the important guarantees in the Bill of Rights came to apply to state as well as federal action. The 
court refers to this process as selective incorporation. 
 
Here are some very basic principles to remember: 
 
1. The guarantees of the Bill of Rights apply only to state and federal government action. They do not limit 
what a company or person in the private sector may do. For example, states may not impose censorship 
on the media or limit free speech in a way that offends the First Amendment, but your boss (in the 
private sector) may order you not to talk to the media. 
2. In some cases, a private company may be regarded as participating in “state action.” For example, a 
private defense contractor that gets 90 percent of its business from the federal government has been

qa_pairs.question: What is the concept of selective incorporation in the context of the Bill of Rights?
qa_pairs.answer: Selective incorporation is a legal doctrine used by the United States Supreme Court to ensure that states and local governments adhere to certain protections guaranteed by the Bill of Rights. Originally, the Bill of Rights was intended to limit only the actions of the federal government. However, over time, the Supreme Court began to apply these rights to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment's due process clause. This clause mandates that states must provide due process in cases affecting the life, liberty, or property of U.S. citizens. The court interprets this requirement as necessitating that states observe certain 'fundamental guarantees' that are considered essential to justice and fairness. As a result, most of the significant protections in the Bill of Rights, such as freedom of speech, the right to a fair trial, and protection against unreasonable searches and seizures, have been incorporated to apply to both state and federal actions. This process ensures that individuals receive consistent protection of their rights across all levels of government.

testing, employees have no constitutional arguments to make; they can simply leave that employer, or

The takings clause of the Fifth Amendment ensures that the government does not take private property 
without just compensation. In the international setting, governments that take private property engage in 
what is called expropriation. The standard under customary international law is that when governments 
do that, they must provide prompt, adequate, and effective compensation. This does not always happen, 
especially where foreign owners’ property is being expropriated. The guarantees of the Fifth Amendment 
(incorporated against state action by the Fourteenth Amendment) are available to property owners where 
state, county, or municipal government uses the power of eminent domain to take private property for 
public purposes. Just what is a public purpose is a matter of some debate. For example, if a city were to 
condemn economically viable businesses or neighborhoods to construct a baseball stadium with public 
money to entice a private enterprise (the baseball team) to stay, is a public purpose being served? 
 
In Kelo v. City of New London, Mrs. Kelo and other residents fought the city of New London, in its 
attempt to use powers of eminent domain to create an industrial park and recreation area that would have 
Pfizer & Co. as a principal tenant. [3] The city argued that increasing its tax base was a sufficient public 
purpose. In a very close decision, the Supreme Court determined that New London’s actions did not 
violate the takings clause. However, political reactions in various states resulted in a great deal of new 
state legislation that would limit the scope of public purpose in eminent domain takings and provide 
additional compensation to property owners in many cases.

qa_pairs.question: What is the standard under customary international law for government expropriation of private property, and how does it relate to the Fifth Amendment's takings clause in the United States?
qa_pairs.answer: Under customary international law, when governments expropriate private property, they are required to provide prompt, adequate, and effective compensation. This principle is mirrored in the Fifth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, which ensures that the government does not take private property without just compensation. The Fifth Amendment's takings clause is incorporated against state action by the Fourteenth Amendment, making it applicable to state, county, or municipal governments. The concept of 'public purpose' is central to eminent domain proceedings, where the government can take private property for public use, provided that just compensation is given. The interpretation of what constitutes a 'public purpose' can be contentious, as seen in cases like Kelo v. City of New London, where the Supreme Court ruled that economic development could be considered a public purpose. However, this decision sparked significant political backlash and led to new state legislation aimed at limiting the scope of public purpose in eminent domain cases and enhancing compensation for property owners.

Since then, the court has employed a two-tiered analysis of substantive due process claims. Under the first 
tier, legislation on economic matters, employment relations, and other business affairs is subject to 
minimal judicial scrutiny. This means that a law will be overturned only if it serves no rational 
government purpose. Under the second tier, legislation concerning fundamental liberties is subject to 
“heightened judicial scrutiny,” meaning that a law will be invalidated unless it is “narrowly tailored to 
serve a significant government purpose.” 
 
The Supreme Court has identified two distinct categories of fundamental liberties. The first category 
includes most of the liberties expressly enumerated in the Bill of Rights. Through a process known as 
selective incorporation, the court has interpreted the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to 
bar states from denying their residents the most important freedoms guaranteed in the first ten 
amendments to the federal Constitution. Only the Third Amendment right (against involuntary 
quartering of soldiers) and the Fifth Amendment right to be indicted by a grand jury have not been made 
applicable to the states. Because these rights are still not applicable to state governments, the Supreme 
Court is often said to have “selectively incorporated” the Bill of Rights into the due process clause of the 
Fourteenth Amendment.

The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) requires that states treat citizens of other states with due process. 
This can be either an issue of procedural due process (as in Section 3.9 "Cases", Burger King v. 
Rudzewicz) or an issue of substantive due process. For substantive due process, consider what happened 
in an Alabama court not too long ago. [5] 
The plaintiff, Dr. Ira Gore, bought a new BMW for $40,000 from a dealer in Alabama. He later discovered 
that the vehicle’s exterior had been slightly damaged in transit from Europe and had therefore been 
repainted by the North American distributor prior to his purchase. The vehicle was, by best estimates, 
worth about 10 percent less than he paid for it. The distributor, BMW of North America, had routinely 
sold slightly damaged cars as brand new if the damage could be fixed for less than 3 percent of the cost of 
the car. In the trial, Dr. Gore sought $4,000 in compensatory damages and also punitive damages. The 
Alabama trial jury considered that BMW was engaging in a fraudulent practice and wanted to punish the 
defendant for a number of frauds it estimated at somewhere around a thousand nationwide. The jury 
awarded not only the $4,000 in compensatory damages but also $4 million in punitive damages, which 
was later reduced to $2 million by the Alabama Supreme Court. On appeal to the US Supreme Court, the 
court found that punitive damages may not be “grossly excessive.” If they are, then they violate 
substantive due process. Whatever damages a state awards must be limited to what is reasonably 
necessary to vindicate the state’s legitimate interest in punishment and deterrence.

protection of the laws.” This is the equal protection clause. It means that, generally speaking, 
governments must treat people equally. Unfair classifications among people or corporations will not be 
permitted. A well-known example of unfair classification would be race discrimination: requiring white

qa_pairs.answer: The Fourteenth Amendment, adopted in 1868, plays a crucial role in ensuring that states treat citizens equally and uphold due process. It mandates that no state shall deny any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws, which means that governments must treat people equally and cannot engage in unfair classifications, such as race discrimination. In the case of Burger King v. Rudzewicz, the Fourteenth Amendment's due process clause was central to the issue of whether the state of Florida could exercise jurisdiction over a Florida resident, Rudzewicz, who had business dealings with a Florida corporation, Burger King. The Supreme Court held that due process requires that a defendant have certain minimum contacts with the forum state such that the maintenance of the suit does not offend traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice. In the case of Dr. Ira Gore's lawsuit against BMW of North America, the Fourteenth Amendment's equal protection clause was invoked when the Alabama jury awarded punitive damages to Dr. Gore for BMW's fraudulent practice of selling slightly damaged cars as brand new. The US Supreme Court later found that punitive damages must not be 'grossly excessive' and must be limited to what is reasonably necessary to vindicate the state's legitimate interest in punishment and deterrence. This case highlighted the importance of substantive due process, which protects individuals from arbitrary and unfair state actions, and the need for punitive damages to be proportionate to the harm caused.

qa_pairs.question: What is the standard of review applied by courts when evaluating government actions under the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, and how does it vary depending on the classification being challenged?
qa_pairs.answer: The standard of review applied by courts when evaluating government actions under the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment varies depending on the classification being challenged. There are three main levels of scrutiny: minimal scrutiny, intermediate scrutiny, and strict scrutiny. Under minimal scrutiny, which is applied to economic and social regulations, laws are presumed valid and will be upheld if they are rationally related to legitimate government goals. For example, a city ordinance limiting the number of street vendors to a rational number would likely be upheld under this standard. Intermediate scrutiny is applied to classifications based on gender. Under this standard, the government must show that the classification serves an important government objective and that the means chosen are substantially related to achieving that objective. A law that discriminates based on gender, such as a city ordinance requiring all street vendors to be women to attract tourism, would need to meet this higher standard to be upheld. Finally, strict scrutiny is applied to classifications based on race, ethnicity, and fundamental rights. Under this most stringent standard, the government must show that the classification serves a compelling government interest and that it is narrowly tailored to achieve that interest. Classifications based on race, ethnicity, or fundamental rights are almost never upheld under strict scrutiny. This tiered approach ensures that classifications that have a more significant impact on individuals' rights are subject to a more rigorous examination.

qa_pairs.question: What would have happened if the Supreme Court had allowed the Connecticut Supreme Court decision to stand?
qa_pairs.answer: If the Supreme Court had allowed the Connecticut Supreme Court decision to stand, it would have set a precedent that state laws could be invalidated based on the right to privacy, even if that right is not explicitly stated in the Constitution. This could have led to a broader interpretation of the Constitution, allowing federal courts to strike down state laws that they deem to violate privacy rights. It would have also shifted the balance of power between the federal government and the states, as states would have less autonomy in legislating on matters that could be subject to federal judicial review. The decision would have relied on the Ninth Amendment, which has historically been used to protect rights not specifically enumerated in the Constitution, but this would have been a novel and controversial use of the amendment. Ultimately, allowing the Connecticut decision to stand would have expanded the scope of the right to privacy and potentially altered the landscape of constitutional law regarding individual liberties and state powers.

qa_pairs.question: What is the principle established by the Supreme Court regarding the balance between state regulations for public health or safety and their impact on interstate commerce under the Commerce Clause?
qa_pairs.answer: The Supreme Court has established that while states have the power to regulate matters of local concern that may affect interstate commerce, this power is not unlimited. The Court has emphasized that a state's power to regulate commerce is always measured against the potential burden on interstate commerce. Regulations that are designed to promote public health or safety can be valid under the Commerce Clause, but they must not interfere with interstate commerce to an extent that outweighs their intended benefits. The Court has developed a balancing test to weigh the asserted safety purpose of a state regulation against the degree of interference with interstate commerce. If the interference is substantial and the safety purpose marginal, the regulation may be invalidated under the Commerce Clause. This principle ensures that while states can address local concerns, they cannot do so in a way that significantly disrupts the national market. The Court's approach requires a careful examination of the state's justification for the regulation and the actual impact on interstate commerce, with a strong presumption of validity for regulations that genuinely aim to protect public health or safety.

qa_pairs.question: What is the purpose of the Austin case in limiting corporate campaign contributions, and was this purpose consistent with the Constitution?
qa_pairs.answer: The Austin case aimed to limit corporate campaign contributions to prevent undue influence on political processes and ensure a level playing field in elections. qa_pairs.question: Does David Lucas have a constitutional cause of action against the South Carolina legislature for effectively 'taking' his property without just compensation, given that the legislation prohibited building beachfront properties to protect the dune system and mitigate hurricane effects?
qa_pairs.answer: David Lucas may have a constitutional cause of action against the South Carolina legislature under the Takings Clause of the Fifth Amendment, which has been applied to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment. The Takings Clause prohibits the government from taking private property for public use without just compensation. Lucas's argument is that the South Carolina legislation, which prohibited building on beachfront properties, effectively took his property by depriving him of its economic use, as he intended to build houses on the parcels he purchased. The South Carolina Coastal Commission's regulations were enacted to protect the dune system and mitigate the effects of hurricanes, which is a legitimate public purpose. However, Lucas could argue that the regulation went too far in diminishing the value of his property without just compensation, thus constituting a regulatory taking. The Supreme Court has established a framework for evaluating regulatory takings claims, which includes considering the economic impact of the regulation, its interference with reasonable investment-backed expectations, and the character of the government action. Lucas's case would likely hinge on whether the court finds that the regulation has gone so far that it constitutes a taking that requires just compensation. The outcome would depend on the specific facts of the case and the court's interpretation of the Takings Clause in the context of Lucas's property rights and the state's interest in environmental protection.

From the 1930s on, administrative agencies, law, and procedures have virtually remade our 
government and much of private life. Every day, business must deal with rules and decisions of state 
and federal administrative agencies. Informally, such rules are often called regulations, and they 
differ (only in their source) from laws passed by Congress and signed into law by the president. The 
rules created by agencies are voluminous: thousands of new regulations pour forth each year. The 
overarching question of whether there is too much regulation—or the wrong kind of regulation—of 
our economic activities is an important one but well beyond the scope of this chapter, in which we 
offer an overview of the purpose of administrative agencies, their structure, and their impact on 
business.

5.1 Administrative Agencies: Their Structure and Powers 
 
LEARNING OBJECTIVES 
 
1. Explain the reasons why we have federal administrative agencies. 
2. Explain the difference between executive branch agencies and independent agencies. 
3. Describe the constitutional issue that questions whether administrative agencies could have authority to 
make enforceable rules that affect business. 
 
 
Why Have Administrative Agencies? 
The US Constitution mentions only three branches of government: legislative, executive, and judicial 
(Articles I, II, and III). There is no mention of agencies in the Constitution, even though federal agencies 
are sometimes referred to as “the fourth branch of government.” The Supreme Court has recognized the 
legitimacy of federal administrative agencies to make rules that have the same binding effect as 
statutes by Congress. 
 
Most commentators note that having agencies with rule-making power is a practical necessity: (1) 
Congress does not have the expertise or continuity to develop specialized knowledge in various areas (e.g., 
communications, the environment, aviation). (2) Because of this, it makes sense for Congress to set forth 
broad statutory guidance to an agency and delegate authority to the agency to propose rules that further 
the statutory purposes. (3) As long as Congress makes this delegating guidance sufficiently clear, it is not 
delegating improperly. If Congress’s guidelines are too vague or undefined, it is (in essence) giving away

qa_pairs.question: What are the reasons for having federal administrative agencies, and how do they differ from independent agencies?
qa_pairs.answer: Federal administrative agencies are established to address the need for specialized knowledge and continuity in various sectors such as communications, the environment, and aviation. Unlike independent agencies, which operate with a higher degree of autonomy from the executive branch, executive branch agencies are directly accountable to the President and are part of the federal government's administrative structure. The Supreme Court has upheld the legitimacy of these agencies, allowing them to create rules with the same binding effect as statutes passed by Congress. The delegation of authority from Congress to these agencies is considered practical and necessary, as Congress lacks the expertise to develop specialized knowledge in all areas. However, for this delegation to be valid, Congress must provide clear and sufficiently defined guidelines. If the guidelines are too vague, it could be seen as an improper delegation of power. In summary, federal administrative agencies are essential for the effective governance of specialized areas, and they differ from independent agencies in their level of autonomy and direct accountability to the President.

Powers of Agencies 
Agencies have a variety of powers. Many of the original statutes that created them, like the Federal 
Communications Act, gave them licensing power. No party can enter into the productive activity covered 
by the act without prior license from the agency—for example, no utility can start up a nuclear power

deregulation of the economy has led to diminution of some licensing power. Many agencies also have the 
authority to set the rates charged by companies subject to the agency’s jurisdiction. Finally, the agencies 
can regulate business practices. The FTC has general jurisdiction over all business in interstate commerce 
to monitor and root out “unfair acts” and “deceptive practices.” The Securities and Exchange Commission 
(SEC) oversees the issuance of corporate securities and other investments and monitors the practices of 
the stock exchanges.

qa_pairs.question: What are the differences in the appointment and removal process of commissioners in independent agencies compared to members of executive branch agencies?
qa_pairs.answer: Independent agencies have commissioners who are appointed for staggered terms, often longer than a typical four-year presidential term, and cannot be removed except for 'good cause.' During the course of the past seventy years, a substantial debate has been conducted, often in shrill 
terms, about the legitimacy of administrative lawmaking. One criticism is that agencies are 
“captured” by the industry they are directed to regulate. Another is that they overregulate, stifling 
individual initiative and the ability to compete. During the 1960s and 1970s, a massive outpouring of 
federal law created many new agencies and greatly strengthened the hands of existing ones. In the 
late 1970s during the Carter administration, Congress began to deregulate American society, and 
deregulation increased under the Reagan administration. But the accounting frauds of WorldCom, 
Enron, and others led to the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, and the financial meltdown of 2008 has 
led to reregulation of the financial sector. It remains to be seen whether the Deepwater Horizon oil 
blowout of 2010 will lead to more environmental regulations or a rethinking on how to make 
agencies more effective regulators. 
 
Administrative agencies are the focal point of controversy because they are policy-making bodies, 
incorporating facets of legislative, executive, and judicial power in a hybrid form that fits uneasily at 
best in the framework of American government (see Figure 5.1 "Major Administrative Agencies of the 
United States"). They are necessarily at the center of tugging and hauling by the legislature, the 
executive branch, and the judiciary, each of which has different means of exercising political control 
over them. In early 1990, for example, the Bush administration approved a Food and Drug 
Administration regulation that limited disease-prevention claims by food packagers, reversing a 
position by the Reagan administration in 1987 permitting such claims.

qa_pairs.question: Why does Congress need to delegate rule-making authority to specialized agencies?
qa_pairs.answer: Congress needs to delegate rule-making authority to specialized agencies for several reasons. Firstly, Congress, as the legislative body, is composed of elected representatives who may not have the time, expertise, or resources to delve into the intricate details of every issue that requires regulation. Specialized agencies, on the other hand, are staffed with experts who have the necessary knowledge and skills to understand complex technical and scientific matters. This expertise ensures that the regulations they create are well-informed and effective in addressing the specific issues at hand. Secondly, delegating rule-making authority allows for more efficient and timely responses to emerging challenges and technological advancements. Specialized agencies can adapt and update regulations more quickly than Congress, which operates through a slower legislative process. This agility is crucial in areas such as environmental protection, public health, and financial regulation, where rapid changes can have significant impacts. Thirdly, specialized agencies can provide a level of continuity and consistency in regulation that might be difficult to achieve through the legislative process. Agencies can build upon previous regulations, refine them over time, and ensure that there is a coherent regulatory framework in place. This continuity helps businesses and individuals to better understand and comply with regulations. Lastly, delegating rule-making authority to specialized agencies can help to balance the power between the legislative and executive branches of government. It allows Congress to set broad policy goals and standards while leaving the detailed implementation to agencies with the appropriate expertise. This division of labor can lead to more effective governance and reduce the likelihood of regulatory capture, where agencies might be unduly influenced by the industries they regulate. Overall, the delegation of rule-making authority to specialized agencies is a practical and necessary aspect of modern governance, enabling Congress to leverage expertise, respond swiftly to new challenges, and maintain a balanced and effective regulatory system.

Legislative Control 
Congress can always pass a law repealing a regulation that an agency promulgates. Because this is a time-
consuming process that runs counter to the reason for creating administrative bodies, it happens rarely. 
Another approach to controlling agencies is to reduce or threaten to reduce their appropriations. By 
retaining ultimate control of the purse strings, Congress can exercise considerable informal control over 
regulatory policy. 
 
Executive Control 
The president (or a governor, for state agencies) can exercise considerable control over agencies that are 
part of his cabinet departments and that are not statutorily defined as independent. Federal agencies, 
moreover, are subject to the fiscal scrutiny of the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), subject to the 
direct control of the president. Agencies are not permitted to go directly to Congress for increases in 
budget; these requests must be submitted through the OMB, giving the president indirect leverage over 
the continuation of administrators’ programs and policies.

jurisdiction to hear claims that the agencies have overstepped their legal authority or have acted in some 
unlawful manner.

situated to judge their own jurisdiction and are experts in rulemaking for those matters delegated to them

actions on several possible bases (see Section 5.5.2 "Strategies for Obtaining Judicial Review" on

qa_pairs.question: What are the various methods through which Congress can exert control over administrative agencies, and how does the president maintain oversight over these agencies?
qa_pairs.answer: Congress can exert control over administrative agencies through several methods. One primary method is by passing legislation that can repeal or modify regulations promulgated by agencies. This legislative process, although time-consuming, serves as a direct means of control. Another method is through the control of appropriations. By managing the budget allocations for agencies, Congress can indirectly influence their operations and policies. This is because agencies must go through the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for budget increases, giving the president indirect leverage over their programs and policies. Additionally, Congress can hold hearings and investigations to scrutinize agency actions and decisions, thereby exerting oversight. The president also maintains oversight over administrative agencies through executive control. The president can direct agencies within his cabinet departments and those not defined as independent. Federal agencies are subject to the fiscal scrutiny of the OMB and the direct control of the president. This allows the president to influence agency actions and ensure they align with the administration's policies and goals. Furthermore, the judiciary can review agency actions to ensure they comply with the law. While courts are generally reluctant to overturn agency decisions, they can do so if agencies overstep their legal authority or act unlawfully. This judicial review process provides another layer of oversight, ensuring that agencies operate within the bounds of their legal mandates.

In 1946, Congress enacted the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). This fundamental statute 
detailed for all federal administrative agencies how they must function when they are deciding cases 
or issuing regulations, the two basic tasks of administration. At the state level, the Model State 
Administrative Procedure Act, issued in 1946 and revised in 1961, has been adopted in twenty-eight 
states and the District of Columbia; three states have adopted the 1981 revision. The other states 
have statutes that resemble the model state act to some degree. 
 
Trial-Type Hearings 
Deciding cases is a major task of many agencies. For example, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is 
empowered to charge a company with having violated the Federal Trade Commission Act. Perhaps a seller 
is accused of making deceptive claims in its advertising. Proceeding in a manner similar to a court, staff 
counsel will prepare a case against the company, which can defend itself through its lawyers. The case is 
tried before an administrative law judge (ALJ), formerly known as an administrative hearing 
examiner. The change in nomenclature was made in 1972 to enhance the prestige of ALJs and more

qa_pairs.question: What is the purpose of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) enacted by Congress in 1946?
qa_pairs.answer: The Administrative Procedure Act (APA) was enacted by Congress in 1946 to establish a comprehensive framework for federal administrative agencies in the United States. Its primary purpose is to ensure that these agencies operate in a fair, transparent, and accountable manner when making decisions or issuing regulations. The APA outlines the procedures that agencies must follow, including how they should conduct hearings, how they should issue rules, and how they should respond to public comments. It also provides for judicial review of agency actions, allowing courts to evaluate whether an agency has acted within its legal authority and followed proper procedures. By doing so, the APA aims to protect the rights of individuals and businesses affected by agency decisions, promote public participation in the rulemaking process, and ensure that agencies do not exceed their statutory mandates. The APA also seeks to enhance the consistency and predictability of administrative actions, thereby fostering a more efficient and effective regulatory environment.

(regulations) must allow for full participation by interested parties. The Administrative Procedure Act (APA) 
governs both rulemaking and the agency enforcement of regulations, and it provides a process for fair 
hearings.

The Paperwork Burden 
The administrative process is not frictionless. The interplay between government agency and private 
enterprise can burden business operations in a number of ways. Several of these are noted in this section. 
 
Deciding whether and how to act are not decisions that government agencies reach out of the blue. They 
rely heavily on information garnered from business itself. Dozens of federal agencies require corporations 
to keep hundreds of types of records and to file numerous periodic reports. The Commission on Federal 
Paperwork, established during the Ford administration to consider ways of reducing the paperwork 
burden, estimated in its final report in 1977 that the total annual cost of federal paperwork amounted to 
$50 billion and that the 10,000 largest business enterprises spent $10 billion annually on paperwork 
alone. The paperwork involved in licensing a single nuclear power plant, the commission said, costs 
upward of $15 million. 
 
Not surprisingly, therefore, businesses have sought ways of avoiding requests for data. Since the 1940s, 
the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has collected economic data on corporate performance from 
individual companies for statistical purposes. As long as each company engages in a single line of 
business, data are comparable. When the era of conglomerates began in the 1970s, with widely divergent

In 1980, responding to cries that businesses, individuals, and state and local governments were being

tax and business records. The OMB was given the power also to determine whether new kinds of 
information are needed. In effect, any agency that wants to collect new information from outside must

Inspections 
No one likes surprise inspections. A section of the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 empowers 
agents of the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) to search work areas for safety 
hazards and for violations of OSHA regulations. The act does not specify whether inspectors are required 
to obtain search warrants, required under the Fourth Amendment in criminal cases. For many years, the 
government insisted that surprise inspections are not unreasonable and that the time required to obtain a 
warrant would defeat the surprise element. The Supreme Court finally ruled squarely on the issue in 1978.

In 1966, Congress enacted the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), opening up to the citizenry many of 
the files of the government. (The act was amended in 1974 and again in 1976 to overcome a tendency of 
many agencies to stall or refuse access to their files.) Under the FOIA, any person has a legally enforceable 
right of access to all government documents, with nine specific exceptions, such as classified military 
intelligence, medical files, and trade secrets and commercial or financial information if “obtained from a 
person and privileged or confidential.” Without the trade-secret and financial-information exemptions,

Neither an administrative agency’s adjudication nor its issuance of a regulation is necessarily final. Most 
federal agency decisions are appealable to the federal circuit courts. To get to court, the appellant must 
overcome numerous complex hurdles. He or she must have standing—that is, be in some sense directly 
affected by the decision or regulation. The case must be ripe for review; administrative remedies such as 
further appeal within the agency must have been exhausted.

must have been a decision reached that was unfavorable to you, and you must have appealed the decision 
to the full board. The full board must rule against you, and only then will you be heard by a court. The 
broadest exception to this exhaustion of administrative remedies requirement is if the agency had

qa_pairs.question: What are the requirements for a party to seek judicial review of an agency's decision in the United States federal court system?
qa_pairs.answer: To seek judicial review of an agency's decision in the United States federal court system, a party must first exhaust all available administrative remedies. This means that the party must have requested a hearing at the hearing examiner level, received a decision from the hearing examiner, and then appealed that decision to the full board of the agency. Only after the full board has ruled against the party can the case be brought before a court. The party must also have standing, meaning they must be directly affected by the agency's decision or regulation. Additionally, the case must be ripe for review, which means that all administrative appeals must have been completed. There are exceptions to the exhaustion requirement, such as when the agency has acted in bad faith, when the administrative remedies are inadequate, or when the remedies would be futile.

Strategies for Obtaining Judicial Review 
Once these obstacles are cleared, the court may look at one of a series of claims. The appellant might 
assert that the agency’s action was ultra vires (UL-truh VI-reez)—beyond the scope of its authority as set 
down in the statute. This attack is rarely successful. A somewhat more successful claim is that the agency 
did not abide by its own procedures or those imposed upon it by the Administrative Procedure Act. 
 
In formal rulemaking, the appellant also might insist that the agency lacked substantial evidence for the 
determination that it made. If there is virtually no evidence to support the agency’s findings, the court 
may reverse. But findings of fact are not often overturned by the courts. 
 
Likewise, there has long been a presumption that when an agency issues a regulation, it has the authority 
to do so: those opposing the regulation must bear a heavy burden in court to upset it. This is not a 
surprising rule, for otherwise courts, not administrators, would be the authors of regulations. 
Nevertheless, regulations cannot exceed the scope of the authority conferred by Congress on the agency. 
In an important 1981 case before the Supreme Court, the issue was whether the secretary of labor, acting 
through the Occupational Health and Safety Administration (OSHA), could lawfully issue a standard 
limiting exposure to cotton dust in the workplace without first undertaking a cost-benefit analysis. A 
dozen cotton textile manufacturers and the American Textile Manufacturers Institute, representing 175 
companies, asserted that the cotton dust standard was unlawful because it did not rationally relate the

"Cases", American Textile Manufacturers Institute v. Donovan.

qa_pairs.question: What are the conditions under which a court may hear an appeal without requiring the exhaustion of administrative remedies according to the provided text?
qa_pairs.answer: A court may hear an appeal without requiring the exhaustion of administrative remedies under several conditions. Firstly, if the agency had no authority to issue the rule or regulation in the first place, the court may bypass the exhaustion requirement. Secondly, if it would be impractical or futile to exhaust administrative remedies, the court may intervene. Thirdly, if great harm would result from the continued application of the rule or regulation, the court may hear the appeal. Additionally, if the agency is not acting in good faith, the courts will hear an appeal without the need for exhaustion of remedies. These exceptions are designed to prevent undue harm or injustice that could result from strictly adhering to the exhaustion requirement.

Mainly for historical reasons, it has always been more difficult to sue the government than to sue private 
individuals or corporations. For one thing, the government has long had recourse to the doctrine of

Procedure Act to waive any federal claim to sovereign immunity in cases of injunctive or other 
nonmonetary relief. Earlier, in 1946, in the Federal Tort Claims Act, Congress had waived sovereign 
immunity of the federal government for most tort claims for money damages, although the act contains 
several exceptions for specific agencies (e.g., one cannot sue for injuries resulting from fiscal operations of 
the Treasury Department or for injuries stemming from activities of the military in wartime). The act also 
contains a major exception for claims “based upon [an official’s] exercise or performance or the failure to 
exercise or perform a discretionary function or duty.” This exception prevents suits against parole boards 
for paroling dangerous criminals who then kill or maim in the course of another crime and suits against 
officials whose decision to ship explosive materials by public carrier leads to mass deaths and injuries 
following an explosion en route. [2] 
 
In recent years, the Supreme Court has been stripping away the traditional immunity enjoyed by many 
government officials against personal suits. Some government employees—judges, prosecutors, 
legislators, and the president, for example—have absolute immunity against suit for official actions. But 
many public administrators and government employees have at best a qualified immunity. Under a 
provision of the Civil Rights Act of 1871 (so-called Section 1983 actions), state officials can be sued in 
federal court for money damages whenever “under color of any state law” they deprive anyone of his 
rights under the Constitution or federal law. In Bivens v. Six Unknown Federal Narcotics Agents, the 
Supreme Court held that federal agents may be sued for violating the plaintiff’s Fourth Amendment rights 
against an unlawful search of his home.[3] Subsequent cases have followed this logic to permit suits for 
violations of other constitutional provisions. This area of the law is in a state of flux, and it is likely to 
continue to evolve.

qa_pairs.question: What legal doctrines and acts have historically protected the government from lawsuits, and how have recent Supreme Court decisions affected the immunity of government officials and employees?
qa_pairs.answer: Historically, the government has been protected from lawsuits by the doctrine of sovereign immunity, which has been a significant barrier to suing the government compared to private individuals or corporations. This doctrine was challenged when Congress amended the Administrative Procedure Act in 1976, waiving federal claims to sovereign immunity in cases seeking injunctive or other nonmonetary relief. Additionally, the Federal Tort Claims Act of 1946 waived sovereign immunity for most tort claims for money damages, with exceptions for specific agencies and discretionary functions. The Supreme Court has recently been eroding the immunity enjoyed by many government officials and employees. While some officials, such as judges, prosecutors, legislators, and the president, have absolute immunity for their official actions, many public administrators and employees have qualified immunity. Under Section 1983 of the Civil Rights Act of 1871, state officials can be sued for violating constitutional or federal rights. The Supreme Court's decision in Bivens v. Six Unknown Federal Narcotics Agents allowed federal agents to be sued for Fourth Amendment violations. This area of law is evolving, with ongoing cases likely to further shape the landscape of government liability.

Sometimes damage is done to an individual or business because the government has given out erroneous 
information. For example, suppose that Charles, a bewildered, disabled navy employee, is receiving a 
federal disability annuity. Under the regulations, he would lose his pension if he took a job that paid him 
in each of two succeeding years more than 80 percent of what he earned in his old navy job. A few years 
later, Congress changed the law, making him ineligible if he earned more than 80 percent in anyone year.

For many years, Charles earned considerably less than the ceiling amount. But then one year he got the 
opportunity to make some extra money. Not wishing to lose his pension, he called an employee relations 
specialist in the US Navy and asked how much he could earn and still keep his pension. The specialist 
gave him erroneous information over the telephone and then sent him an out-of-date form that said 
Charles could safely take on the extra work. Unfortunately, as it turned out, Charles did exceed the salary 
limit, and so the government cut off his pension during the time he earned too much. Charles sues to 
recover his lost pension. He argues that he relied to his detriment on false information supplied by the 
navy and that in fairness the government should be estopped from denying his claim. 
 
Unfortunately for Charles, he will lose his case. In Office of Personnel Management v. Richmond, the 
Supreme Court reasoned that it would be unconstitutional to permit recovery. [4] The appropriations 
clause of Article I says that federal money can be paid out only through an appropriation made by law. 
The law prevented this particular payment to be made. If the court were to make an exception, it would 
permit executive officials in effect to make binding payments, even though unauthorized, simply by 
misrepresenting the facts. The harsh reality, therefore, is that mistakes of the government are generally 
held against the individual, not the government, unless the law specifically provides for recompense (as, 
for example, in the Federal Tort Claims Act just discussed).

qa_pairs.question: What are the conditions under which a search of private property, including commercial premises, is considered 'unreasonable' according to the Supreme Court ruling in Camara v. Municipal Court?
qa_pairs.answer: A search of private property, including commercial premises, is considered 'unreasonable' unless it has been authorized by a valid search warrant, except in certain carefully defined classes of cases. The Court stated that the basic purpose of the Fourth Amendment is to safeguard the privacy and security of individuals against arbitrary invasions by governmental officials. Therefore, unless there is a valid search warrant, the privacy interest of individuals is violated when the government intrudes on their property, regardless of whether the motivation is to investigate criminal law violations or breaches of other statutory or regulatory standards.

qa_pairs.question: Is the provision for warrantless inspections by the Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) constitutional?
qa_pairs.answer: The constitutionality of the Mine Safety and Health Administration's (MSHA) provision for warrantless inspections, as authorized by the Federal Mine Safety and Health Amendments Act of 1977, has been a subject of legal scrutiny. The Act allows MSHA to conduct up to four warrantless inspections per year to ensure that safety violations have been corrected. The Supreme Court has previously addressed the issue of warrantless inspections in the context of the Fourth Amendment, which protects against unreasonable searches and seizures. In the case of Marshall v. Barlow's, Inc., the Court held that the Occupational Safety and Health Act (OSHA) did not authorize warrantless inspections of private businesses. However, OSHA was later amended to allow for warrantless inspections, and the Supreme Court upheld this provision in Marshall v. Barlow's, Inc. The Court reasoned that the need for effective enforcement of safety regulations justified the warrantless inspections. MSHA's inspections are similar to those authorized by OSHA, and it is likely that the Supreme Court would find MSHA's warrantless inspections to be constitutional, given the precedent set by OSHA's similar provisions. The Court would consider whether the inspections are reasonable and whether they serve a significant government interest in protecting worker safety. If MSHA's inspections are found to be reasonable and necessary for the enforcement of safety regulations, the provision for warrantless inspections would likely be deemed constitutional.

qa_pairs.question: Did the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) act arbitrarily and capriciously in adopting a zero-release assumption for nuclear waste storage?
qa_pairs.answer: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) faced legal challenges for adopting a zero-release assumption in its environmental impact statement (EIS) for nuclear waste storage, which assumed that the permanent storage of certain nuclear waste would have no significant environmental impact and that potential storage leakages should not be a factor in the EIS. An environmental NGO sued the NRC, arguing that it had violated regulations by ignoring the potential for contamination. The court of appeals agreed with the NGO, stating that the NRC had acted arbitrarily and capriciously. The NRC had considered the zero-release assumption uncertain and had acknowledged the remote possibility of contamination by water leakage into the storage facility. The court's decision suggests that the NRC's failure to adequately address the potential risks associated with nuclear waste storage in its EIS was not in line with the regulatory requirements. The NRC's actions were deemed to lack a rational basis and to disregard substantial evidence, which are key factors in determining whether an agency has acted arbitrarily and capriciously. The court's ruling implies that the NRC should have provided a more thorough analysis of the potential environmental impacts of nuclear waste storage, including the possibility of leakage and contamination, to comply with the EIS regulations.

qa_pairs.question: Which branch of government is the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) part of?
qa_pairs.answer: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is part of the executive branch of government. The FTC is an independent agency of the United States government, created by Congress to enforce antitrust laws and promote consumer protection. As an executive agency, it operates under the authority of the President and is responsible for regulating business practices to ensure fair competition and protect consumers from unfair, deceptive, or fraudulent practices. The FTC's role in enforcing antitrust laws involves investigating and taking action against companies that engage in monopolistic practices, price fixing, and other activities that harm consumers and competition. The agency also develops and enforces consumer protection laws, conducts research on economic trends, and educates consumers and businesses about their rights and responsibilities. The FTC's status as part of the executive branch means that it is subject to the oversight of the President and Congress, and its actions are guided by the policies and priorities of the executive branch.

qa_pairs.question: Where do proposed rules originally appear in the Clean Water Act?
qa_pairs.answer: In the Clean Water Act, proposed rules originally appear in the Federal Register. The Federal Register is the official journal of the federal government of the United States, in which government agencies publish proposed and final rules, executive orders, proclamations, and other documents of general public interest. When the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), which is responsible for implementing the Clean Water Act, proposes new regulations or amendments to existing regulations, these proposals are first published in the Federal Register. This publication allows for public comment and participation in the rulemaking process, ensuring transparency and accountability. After the public comment period, the EPA reviews the feedback and may revise the proposed rules before finalizing them. Once finalized, the rules are published in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), which is the codification of the general and permanent rules published in the Federal Register by the executive departments and agencies of the federal government.

qa_pairs.question: What is the legal basis for all administrative law, including regulations of the Federal Trade Commission?
qa_pairs.answer: The legal basis for all administrative law, including regulations of the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), is found in the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). The APA is a federal statute that governs the process by which federal agencies develop and issue regulations. It includes requirements for publishing notices of proposed and final rulemaking in the Federal Register, providing opportunities for public comment, and establishing procedures for judicial review of agency actions. The APA also outlines the standards for agency decision-making, ensuring that agencies act within the scope of their authority and follow fair and rational processes. The FTC, as an independent regulatory agency, must comply with the APA when creating and enforcing regulations. The APA's provisions are designed to ensure that administrative agencies, like the FTC, operate in a manner that is transparent, accountable, and consistent with the principles of due process. By adhering to the APA, the FTC and other agencies are required to provide a clear rationale for their regulations, consider public input, and allow for judicial oversight to prevent arbitrary or capricious actions.

Unlike civil actions, where plaintiffs seek compensation or other remedies for themselves, crimes 
involve “the state” (the federal government, a state government, or some subunit of state 
government). This is because crimes involve some “harm to society” and not just harm to certain 
individuals. But “harm to society” is not always evident in the act itself. For example, two friends of 
yours at a party argue, take the argument outside, and blows are struck; one has a bloody nose and 
immediately goes home. The crimes of assault and battery have been committed, even though no one 
else knows about the fight and the friends later make up. By contrast, suppose a major corporation 
publicly announces that it is closing operations in your community and moving operations to 
Southeast Asia. There is plenty of harm to society as the plant closes down and no new jobs take the 
place of the company’s jobs. Although the effects on society are greater in the second example, only 
the first example is a crime. 
 
Crimes are generally defined by legislatures, in statutes; the statutes describe in general terms the 
nature of the conduct they wish to criminalize. For government punishment to be fair, citizens must 
have clear notice of what is criminally prohibited. Ex post facto laws—laws created “after the fact” to 
punish an act that was legal at the time—are expressly prohibited by the US Constitution. Overly 
vague statutes can also be struck down by courts under a constitutional doctrine known as “void for 
vagueness.”

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between a crime and a civil action, and how does the concept of 'harm to society' play a role in determining whether an act is considered a crime?
qa_pairs.answer: A crime is an act that is prohibited by law and is punishable by the state, whereas a civil action involves a lawsuit where the plaintiff seeks compensation or other remedies for harm done to themselves. The key difference lies in the involvement of the state; crimes involve harm to society, not just to individuals. For example, two friends fighting at a party and causing harm to each other is a crime, but it does not involve harm to society. On the other hand, if a major corporation announces it is closing operations in a community, causing widespread unemployment, it is considered a crime because it involves harm to society. The concept of 'harm to society' is crucial in determining whether an act is considered a crime. It is not always evident in the act itself, but it can be inferred from the consequences of the act. For instance, the closure of a major corporation causing unemployment is considered a crime because it harms society, even though no one else directly witnesses the act. In contrast, the same act of closing a corporation would not be considered a crime if it did not cause harm to society. Therefore, the concept of 'harm to society' plays a significant role in determining whether an act is considered a crime.

Most classifications of crime turn on the seriousness of the act. In general, seriousness is defined by the 
nature or duration of the punishment set out in the statute. A felony is a crime punishable (usually) by

usually known as misdemeanors, petty offenses, or infractions. Another way of viewing crimes is by the 
type of social harm the statute is intended to prevent or deter, such as offenses against the person,

All other homicides are criminal. The most severely punished form is murder, defined as homicide 
committed with “malice aforethought.” This is a term with a very long history. Boiled down to its 
essentials, it means that the defendant had the intent to kill. A killing need not be premeditated for any 
long period of time; the premeditation might be quite sudden, as in a bar fight that escalates in that 
moment when one of the fighters reaches for a knife with the intent to kill. 
 
Sometimes a homicide can be murder even if there is no intent to kill; an intent to inflict great bodily 
harm can be murder if the result is the death of another person. A killing that takes place while a felony 
(such as armed robbery) is being committed is also murder, whether or not the killer intended any harm. 
This is the so-called felony murder rule. Examples are the accidental discharge of a gun that kills an 
innocent bystander or the asphyxiation death of a fireman from smoke resulting from a fire set by an 
arsonist. The felony murder rule is more significant than it sounds, because it also applies to the 
accomplices of one who does the killing. Thus the driver of a getaway car stationed a block away from the 
scene of the robbery can be convicted of murder if a gun accidentally fires during the robbery and 
someone is killed. Manslaughter is an act of killing that does not amount to murder. Voluntary 
manslaughter is an intentional killing, but one carried out in the “sudden heat of passion” as the result of 
some provocation. An example is a fight that gets out of hand. Involuntary manslaughter entails a lesser 
degree of willfulness; it usually occurs when someone has taken a reckless action that results in death 
(e.g., a death resulting from a traffic accident in which one driver recklessly runs a red light).

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between justifiable homicide, excusable homicide, and murder in the context of homicide classifications?
qa_pairs.answer: Justifiable homicide is considered a lawful killing, such as in self-defense, where the death is deemed the result of justifiable actions. Excusable homicide, on the other hand, occurs when death results from an accident where the killer is not at fault, such as a tragic mishap. Murder is the most severely punished form of homicide and is defined as a killing committed with 'malice aforethought,' meaning the defendant had the intent to kill. Premeditation is not required for murder; it can occur in a sudden moment, such as during a bar fight. Additionally, a killing can be classified as murder even without the intent to kill if there is an intent to inflict great bodily harm, or if the killing occurs during the commission of a felony, known as the felony murder rule. This rule applies to accomplices as well, making them liable for murder if a death occurs during the felony they were involved in, regardless of their direct intent to harm. Manslaughter is a lesser offense than murder, with voluntary manslaughter involving an intentional killing in the heat of passion due to provocation, and involuntary manslaughter involving a reckless action that unintentionally results in death.

The separate elements of this offense have given rise to all kinds of difficult cases. Take the theft of fruit, 
for example, with regard to the essential element of “personal property.” If a man walking through an 
orchard plucks a peach from a tree and eats it, he is not guilty of larceny because he has not taken away 
personal property (the peach is part of the land, being connected to the tree). But if he picks up a peach 
lying on the ground, he is guilty of larceny. Or consider the element of “taking” or “carrying away.” 
Sneaking into a movie theater without paying is not an act of larceny (though in most states it is a criminal 
act). Taking electricity by tapping into the power lines of an electric utility was something that baffled 
judges late in the nineteenth century because it was not clear whether electricity is a “something” that can 
be taken. Modern statutes have tended to make clear that electricity can be the object of larceny. Or 
consider the element of an “intent to steal the same.” If you borrow your friend’s BMW without his 
permission in order to go to the grocery store, intending to return it within a few minutes and then do 
return it, you have not committed larceny. But if you meet another friend at the store who convinces you 
to take a long joyride with the car and you return hours later, you may have committed larceny. 
 
A particular form of larceny is robbery, which is defined as larceny from a person by means of violence 
or intimidation. 
 
Larceny involves the taking of property from the possession of another. Suppose that a person legitimately 
comes to possess the property of another and wrongfully appropriates it—for example, an automobile 
mechanic entrusted with your car refuses to return it, or a bank teller who is entitled to temporary 
possession of cash in his drawer takes it home with him. The common law had trouble with such cases 
because the thief in these cases already had possession; his crime was in assuming ownership. Today, 
such wrongful conversion, known as embezzlement, has been made a statutory offense in all states.

qa_pairs.question: What is the definition of larceny according to the provided text, and how does it differ from embezzlement?
qa_pairs.answer: Larceny is defined as the wrongful taking and carrying away of the personal property of another with the intent to steal it. This definition includes the essential elements of taking and carrying away personal property with the intent to permanently deprive the owner of it. Embezzlement, on the other hand, involves the wrongful conversion of property that one has been entrusted with. Unlike larceny, embezzlement does not necessarily involve the initial taking of the property; instead, it occurs when someone who has been given possession of the property by another person wrongfully appropriates it for their own use. The common law initially struggled with cases of embezzlement because the thief already had possession of the property, and their crime was in assuming ownership. Today, embezzlement is recognized as a statutory offense in all states, addressing the gaps in the law that larceny and robbery statutes did not cover.

Statutes against larceny and embezzlement did not cover all the gaps in the law. A conceptual problem 
arises in the case of one who is tricked into giving up his title to property. In larceny and embezzlement, 
the thief gains possession or ownership without any consent of the owner or custodian of the property. 
Suppose, however, that an automobile dealer agrees to take his customer’s present car as a trade-in. The 
customer says that he has full title to the car. In fact, the customer is still paying off an installment loan

and the finance company has an interest in the old car. If the finance company repossesses the car, the 
customer—who got a new car at a discount because of his false representation—cannot be said to have 
taken the new car by larceny or embezzlement. Nevertheless, he tricked the dealer into selling, and the 
dealer will have lost the value of the repossessed car. Obviously, the customer is guilty of a criminal act; 
the statutes outlawing it refer to this trickery as the crime of false pretenses, defined as obtaining 
ownership of the property of another by making untrue representations of fact with intent to defraud. 
 
A number of problems have arisen in the judicial interpretation of false-pretense statutes. One concerns 
whether the taking is permanent or only temporary. The case of State v. Mills (Section 6.7 "Cases") shows 
the subtle questions that can be presented and the dangers inherent in committing “a little fraud.” 
 
In the Mills case, the claim was that a mortgage instrument dealing with one parcel of land was used 
instead for another. This is a false representation of fact. Suppose, by contrast, that a person 
misrepresents his state of mind: “I will pay you back tomorrow,” he says, knowing full well that he does 
not intend to. Can such a misrepresentation amount to false pretenses punishable as a criminal offense? 
In most jurisdictions it cannot. A false-pretense violation relates to a past event or existing fact, not to a 
statement of intention. If it were otherwise, anyone failing to pay a debt might find himself facing criminal 
prosecution, and business would be less prone to take risks. 
 
The problem of proving intent is especially difficult when a person has availed himself of the services of 
another without paying. A common example is someone leaving a restaurant without paying for the meal.

qa_pairs.question: What is the crime of false pretenses and how does it differ from larceny and embezzlement?
qa_pairs.answer: The crime of false pretenses involves obtaining ownership of another's property by making untrue representations of fact with the intent to defraud. Unlike larceny and embezzlement, where the thief gains possession or ownership without the owner's consent, false pretenses involve tricking the owner into willingly transferring ownership based on false information. For example, if a customer falsely claims full ownership of a car to trade it in, while still owing money on it, the customer has committed false pretenses. This crime is distinct because it specifically addresses situations where the victim is deceived into transferring ownership, whereas larceny and embezzlement do not involve such deception.

Revenue Service uncovered many instances of bribes paid by major corporations to officials of foreign 
governments to win contracts with those governments. Congress responded in 1977 with the Foreign

In 1970 Congress enacted the Racketeering Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act (RICO), aimed at 
ending organized crime’s infiltration into legitimate business. The act tells courts to construe its language 
broadly “to effectuate its remedial purpose,” and many who are not part of organized crime have been

least two acts within ten years of any of a variety of already-existing crimes, including mail, wire, and 
securities fraud. The act thus makes many types of fraud subject to severe penalties.

qa_pairs.question: How can a corporation be held criminally liable for actions committed by its agents, even though it is not a person?
qa_pairs.answer: A corporation can be held criminally liable for actions committed by its agents through the legal doctrine of vicarious liability. This principle holds that a corporation can be responsible for the criminal acts of its employees or agents if those acts were performed within the scope of their employment or agency. The rationale behind this doctrine is that corporations, as legal entities, have the power to control and direct the actions of their employees, and therefore, they should bear the consequences of those actions. For a corporation to be held liable, it must be proven that the criminal act was committed by an agent of the corporation, and that the act was related to the agent's duties or was done with the intent to benefit the corporation. The prosecution must also establish that the corporation had the opportunity to prevent the criminal act, either through direct oversight or by failing to implement adequate policies and procedures to prevent such conduct. This approach ensures that corporations are incentivized to maintain proper oversight and control over their operations to avoid criminal liability.

To be guilty of a crime, you must have acted. Mental desire or intent to do so is insufficient. But what 
constitutes an act? This question becomes important when someone begins to commit a crime, or 
does so in association with others, or intends to do one thing but winds up doing something else. 
 
Attempt 
It is not necessary to commit the intended crime to be found guilty of a criminal offense. An attempt to 
commit the crime is punishable as well, though usually not as severely. For example, Brett points a gun at 
Ashley, intending to shoot her dead. He pulls the trigger but his aim is off, and he misses her heart by four 
feet. He is guilty of an attempt to murder. Suppose, however, that earlier in the day, when he was 
preparing to shoot Ashley, Brett had been overheard in his apartment muttering to himself of his 
intention, and that a neighbor called the police. When they arrived, he was just snapping his gun into his 
shoulder holster. 
 
At that point, courts in most states would not consider him guilty of an attempt because he had not passed 
beyond the stage of preparation. After having buttoned his jacket he might have reconsidered and put the 
gun away. Determining when the accused has passed beyond mere preparation and taken an actual step 
toward perpetrating the crime is often difficult and is usually for the jury to decide. 
 
Impossibility 
What if a defendant is accused of attempting a crime that is factually impossible? For example, suppose 
that men believed they were raping a drunken, unconscious woman, and were later accused of attempted 
rape, but defended on the grounds of factual impossibility because the woman was actually dead at the 
time sexual intercourse took place? Or suppose that a husband intended to poison his wife with 
strychnine in her coffee, but put sugar in the coffee instead? The “mens rea” or criminal intent was there, 
but the act itself was not criminal (rape requires a live victim, and murder by poisoning requires the use of 
Saylor URL: http://www.saylor.org/books 
 
Saylor.org 
 
 
256 
poison). States are divided on this, but thirty-seven states have ruled out factual impossibility as a defense 
to the crime of attempt.

qa_pairs.question: What is the significance of intention in criminal law, and how does it affect the prosecution of criminal attempts?
qa_pairs.answer: In criminal law, intention plays a crucial role in determining guilt and the severity of punishment. The concept of 'mens rea,' or criminal intent, is fundamental to establishing that a person committed a crime. For an act to be considered criminal, there must be both a guilty act ('actus reus') and a guilty mind ('mens rea'). Intention refers to the mental desire or intent to commit a crime. However, merely having the intention to commit a crime is not enough to be found guilty; there must be an act that constitutes the crime itself. This is where the concept of attempt comes into play. An attempt to commit a crime is punishable, even if the crime is not completed. For example, if someone intends to commit murder but misses the target, they can still be charged with an attempt to murder. The law recognizes that the intention to commit a crime is a significant step towards its commission, and punishing attempts serves as a deterrent to prevent individuals from progressing towards criminal acts. However, the determination of when an individual has moved beyond mere preparation and has taken a substantial step towards committing the crime can be complex. Courts often rely on the jury to decide if the accused has crossed the threshold from preparation to attempt. Additionally, the concept of impossibility can complicate matters. If a defendant attempts a crime that is factually impossible, such as trying to poison someone with sugar instead of poison, the defense may argue that no crime was committed. However, the presence of criminal intent ('mens rea') can still result in a conviction for an attempt, as the law focuses on the intent to commit a crime rather than the feasibility of the act itself. Different states have varying rules regarding the defense of factual impossibility, with some allowing it as a defense and others not. Overall, intention is a key element in criminal law, as it helps to establish the culpability of individuals and ensures that those who attempt to commit crimes are held accountable for their actions.

Conspiracy 
Under both federal and state laws, it is a separate offense to work with others toward the commission of a 
crime. When two or more people combine to carry out an unlawful purpose, they are engaged in a 
conspiracy. The law of conspiracy is quite broad, especially when it is used by prosecutors in connection 
with white-collar crimes. Many people can be swept up in the net of conspiracy, because it is unnecessary 
to show that the actions they took were sufficient to constitute either the crime or an attempt. Usually, the 
prosecution needs to show only (1) an agreement and (2) a single overt act in furtherance of the 
conspiracy. Thus if three people agree to rob a bank, and if one of them goes to a store to purchase a gun 
to be used in the holdup, the three can be convicted of conspiracy to commit robbery. Even the purchase 
of an automobile to be used as the getaway car could support a conspiracy conviction. 
 
The act of any one of the conspirators is imputed to the other members of the conspiracy. It does not 
matter, for instance, that only one of the bank robbers fired the gun that killed a guard. All can be 
convicted of murder. That is so even if one of the conspirators was stationed as a lookout several blocks 
away and even if he specifically told the others that his agreement to cooperate would end “just as soon as 
there is shooting.”
